answer: In a V12 decision record a hard constraint is a gating condition a candidate must satisfy, while a soft constraint is only a preference that can be traded. A candidate that fails a hard constraint is eliminated outright, even if it is best on every other metric: the decision-record contract says that if candidate C exceeds a declared cost ceiling it is eliminated even though it has the highest success rate, and in the worked example C is eliminated by the hard cost and p95-latency constraints while A and B pass and are then compared. The record's decision tree encodes the same asymmetry: 'Hard constraints pass?' - No - 'Eliminate candidate'; only survivors are compared on success and cost, and trade-offs happen there. So a failed hard constraint removes the candidate from consideration rather than costing it points, whereas soft preferences are traded off among surviving candidates. Hard, soft and non-quantitative constraints are kept in separate fields precisely so a weighted composite score cannot hide or trade away a hard constraint. A non-quantitative constraint the model cannot measure (for example operability) does not eliminate a candidate; if it remains unverified the record keeps the recommendation conditional and records reversal triggers, which is a different treatment from both a failed hard constraint and an ordinary soft preference.
